bib.title: Understanding Social Reasoning in Language Models with Language Models
bib.venue: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks

question: Can theory-of-mind (ToM) evaluations be generated procedurally by an LLM filling causal templates, with control conditions, so that LLM social reasoning can be measured more validly than with earlier crowd-sourced or expert-written tests?
hypothesis: Model-populated causal templates yield evaluations of quality comparable to expert-written ones, and the template conditions expose where LLMs fail ToM inference; the authors also hypothesise that circularity (test-taker also being the generator) is not a confound.
contributions: A framework for generating systematic evaluations from causal templates, with control conditions, via automated tests.
Showing that the scalable, cost-efficient method yields quality comparable to crowd-sourced and expert-written tests (human ratings).
Testing ToM reasoning in a variety of LLMs with different prompting techniques and comparing with human performance.

method.summary: A causal template (context, desire, percept, belief, causal event, aware/unaware percepts, actions, questions, answers, random event) is turned into a prompt; gpt-4-0314 populates the variables for 200 templates; code stitches variables into 25 conditions per template (5,000 items). Quality is rated by experts and 200 Prolific participants against socialIQa and expert items; six LLMs are evaluated with 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 1-shot, 1-shot CoT prompts and compared to 20 human participants.
method.task: Theory-of-mind multiple-choice (two options) story comprehension: forward belief, forward action, backward belief inference, with true-belief/false-belief and with/without initial belief variants, plus random-event controls

datasets.name: BigToM
datasets.size: 200 templates x 25 conditions = 5,000 test items (24 conditions with causal or random event plus condition 25 initial percept to initial belief)
datasets.split: main results on 6 conditions (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief; TB and FB), each with and without initial belief; rest in appendix
datasets.source: generated by gpt-4-0314; released under MIT License
datasets.preprocessing: templates rejected if they do not follow assigned structure (gpt-4 fails structure ~2-3% of the time); exactly one sentence per variable

datasets.name: BigToM-Claude
datasets.source: generated by Claude-2 with the same procedure

datasets.name: Expert items (quality comparison)
datasets.size: 50 items: Kosinski (21 of 40), Ullman (9 of 9), Dodell-Feder / Moghaddam and Honey (remaining)

other.use: populates templates (temperature 0.5, default other parameters) and is evaluated (temperature 0)
generates BigToM-Claude; evaluated on both sets

other.hardware: single NVIDIA A40 GPU, internal cluster, via llama.cpp

inference.decoding: temperature 0 for evaluated models; generation uses gpt-4-0314 at temperature 0.5
inference.samples: Template generation: 3 new completions per prompt using 3 few-shot examples. Evaluation: one deterministic run per item (temperature 0); number of runs/seeds not stated.
inference.prompting: 0-shot, 0-shot-CoT, 1-shot, 1-shot-CoT; chat models get instructions as system message and question as user message; the 1-shot example is from Forward Belief - False Belief (Kofi fishing net); answer format 'Answer:<option>)<answer>'

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of two-option questions answered correctly; false-belief score reported as TB∧FB: counted only if the model also succeeded on the true-belief version

metrics.name: human quality rating
metrics.definition: three 1-5 Likert items (understandability, unambiguous, coherent question and answer); aggregate = mean of the three

baselines: Human participants (20, Prolific, 'with initial belief' version of 3 main conditions)
eval.protocol: Quality: 2 experts (authors) rated 100 templates (2500 items); 200 Prolific participants each rated 30 items (10 FB-true, 10 FB-false, 5 Expert, 5 socialIQa), 20 ratings per item on 200 BigToM items; Bayesian linear mixed-effects model with dataset fixed effect and random effects for items and participants. Circularity check: logistic regression of correctness on data source and model.

availability.code: prompts and evaluation scripts released on project page https://sites.google.com/view/social-reasoning-lms

prompts.text: Answer the questions based on the context. Keep your answer concise, few words are enough, maximum one sentence. Answer as ’Answer:<option>)<answer>’

Answer the questions based on the context. Reason step by step before answering in ’Thought: Let’s think step by step’. Write your final answer as ’Answer:<option>)<answer>’. Always pick an option, do not say none of the above or that there is not enough information.

Story: Kofi is a fisherman from a small village in Ghana. He wants to catch enough fish today to provide for his family and sell the surplus at the market. Kofi repaired his fishing net last night. While Kofi is away from his boat, a group of monkeys comes and plays with the fishing net, tearing it apart. Kofi does not see the monkeys damaging his fishing net Question: Does Kofi believe his fishing net is in good condition or torn apart? Choose one of the following: a)Kofi believes his fishing net is in good condition. b)Kofi believes his fishing net is torn apart.

Generate new stories based on the following template. (full prompt: Fig. 4 lists fields Context, Prior: Desire, Percept, Belief, Causal Event, Percepts aware/not aware, Actions, Questions, Answers, Random Event; instructs to be creative, diverse, uncommon names)

results.claim: Dataset diversity: GPT-4 annotation of 200 templates gives counts of 154, 76 and 7 for changeable states, mechanisms of change and mediums of perception.

limits: Evaluation may seem circular because GPT-4 writes the items; authors check with a Claude-2-generated set of only 30 templates / 750 conditions.
Generated items can be biased and stereotyped and syntactically similar, reducing diversity; ~3% of stories contain commonsense errors.
Only first-order belief in main results (second-order only sketched, Fig. 15); stories are short, traditional ToM tests, not realistic deployments.
Human baseline is 20 participants on the with-initial-belief version only; human accuracy for forward belief/action appears only in figures.
1-shot CoT gains may reflect imitating the reasoning template rather than ToM.
Models are 2023 snapshots (gpt-4-0314, claude-v1.3, text-davinci-003) and have dated; number of runs per prompt is not stated and no confidence intervals are given for model accuracy.
Quality human study rated only the Forward Belief TB and FB conditions as exemplars.
